passage:
Every Saturday at the Kishanganj block office, the free health camp began with the same queue. Suraj, a second-year volunteer, sat with a register copying each patient's name, age and village, then a second volunteer copied it again onto the doctor's sheet. The queue moved at a crawl in the heat.
Samir, the camp coordinator, said, "Can you write faster?"
Suraj thought about it on the bus home. Faster wasn't the answer. The copying itself was the problem. Why write everything twice?
Next Saturday he stuck a printed QR code at the gate. Most families had one smartphone. They scanned it and filled a short form, and the list appeared on the doctor's tablet directly. For those without phones, Suraj typed the details himself, once.
By ten o'clock the queue was half its usual length. Samir looked at the tablet and shook his head, smiling. "No register at all?"

qa.q: Where did Suraj stick the printed QR code?
How might Suraj have felt when Samir asked him to write faster?
qa.a: He probably felt pressured and a little frustrated, which led him to question the copying itself on the bus home.

qa.q: Why was removing the copying step better than trying to write faster?
qa.a: Because writing faster could only save a little time, while removing the double copying cut the queue to half.

qa.q: How might families without smartphones experience the new check-in?
qa.a: They still get registered, since Suraj types their details once, so no one is left out.

grounding: It shows a student volunteer replacing a copied attendance register with a QR check-in that removes the copying step entirely.

subtype: Approach: changes the question from making it faster to removing the step [Action]
passage:
At the Saturday football club in Leeds, Liam had been the volunteer on the clipboard for a year. Every child's name ticked on paper, then typed into a spreadsheet on Sunday night for the council grant report. Two hours of copying, every week.
Vera, the club secretary, asked him in September, "Can you get the typing done faster? The grant deadline moved up."
Liam almost said yes. Then he stopped. "What if there's no typing at all?"
He made a QR code linked to a simple sign-in form and taped it to the pavilion door. Parents scanned it at drop-off. The names went straight into the sheet.
On the first Saturday, three parents asked for help, and one little boy scanned it himself.
On Sunday night, Liam opened the sheet. Everything was already there. He texted Vera: "Report's done. Took four minutes."

qa.q: Where did Liam tape the QR code?
qa.a: He taped it to the pavilion door.

qa.q: How do you think Liam felt when he opened the sheet on Sunday night?
qa.a: He probably felt relieved and pleased, since two hours of copying had shrunk to four minutes.

qa.q: What else could Liam do to help parents who find the QR code hard?
qa.a: He could keep a paper list for a few weeks and enter those names himself, so no child is missed while people get used to it.

qa.q: How might Vera see Liam's message on Sunday night?
qa.a: Vera may be surprised and delighted, since she only asked for faster typing and got a finished report.

grounding: It shows a volunteer asking to remove the copying step rather than speed it up, replacing a paper sign-in with a QR check-in.
